newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish cement sales seen up 5 pct in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Polish cement sales seen up 5 pct in 1997.

text.p: Sales of cement in Poland are likely to rise five percent this year after a 4.4 percent increase to 14 million tonnes in 1996, cement industry officials said on Monday.

They told a news conference data on total cement sales last year, including exports, was less optimistic at just above one percent growth, because of a 10 percent drop of its exports to Germany -- the buyer of 95 percent of Poland's cement exports.

"Because in 1996 cement consumption there weakened, the Germans began producing more of their own cement and because the zloty exchange rate was unfavourable our cement exports fell almost 10 percent," said Andrzej Balcerek, head of the Gorazdze cement plant.
"However, this was fortunately compenstated by a rise in domestic demand, which conservative estimates show will grow five percent this year," he added.
He said Poland's 15-year programme of building 2,600 km of motorways would give cement sales a strong boost.

"Depending on the technology used, the motorways programme will consume a total of between 10 and 13 million tonnes of cement," Balcerek said adding that the production potential of the whole sector was 17-18 million tonnes.
Poland has 20 cement plants and nine lime factories, 90 percent of which have already been privatised.

Andrzej Tekiel, head of the Malogoszcz cement plant, said French concern Lafarge, which has three Polish plants, leads the sector with a 22.7 percent market share while Belgian-German Heidelberger-CBR, with two cement plants has 18 percent.

The Ozarow cement plant, owned by Polish Cement Holding SA in which Ireland's CRH has a stake, comes third with a 14.5 percent share and Germany's Miebach, which has two plants is fourth with 10 percent.
The other companies, including Germany's Dyckerhoff, Turkey's Rumeli Group and British Readymix have between two and 4.5 percent shares in the market, Tekli said.

Balcerek said the sector as a whole made a very small profit in 1996 mostly thanks to three cement plants which used modern, cost-effective dry technology, while many of the older wet-technology plants made a loss.
He declined to give any specifc figures.
